origin: decision D31, second correction round (noted by the corrector, outside its findings)
problem: A test can still be moved as `pending` after its flag has been turned on in the repository's definitions; nothing refuses it until a later removal story names it.
proposed_resolution: Have F-STATES refuse a new `pending` move for a flag whose definition already serves the on value, or have the turn-on check run again when such a move is made.

outcome.what_was_done: Recorded by the orchestrating session from the corrector's notes. No further round of design fixes is run on D31; the package named in the triage settles it when it is built.

problem: Nothing stops a flag from being wrapped around a change that turning the flag off cannot undo: a schema change or data migration, data written in a new format while the flag is on, a message sent or an outside call made. No duty (story-writer, implementer), no review item and no check names it. F-ITEMS' flag-off item asks whether new code is reachable with the flag off; it does not ask about effects made while the flag was on. The design also promises the opposite. The pull request's Rollback section says that after the flag is turned off 'the product behaves as it did before the change', and the release packet gives the kill switch as the way to roll a flag back. Take a flagged story whose on path writes a new stored format. Turning the flag off leaves the old code reading data it cannot parse. Its flag_off tests still pass at red and at green, because they run on fresh test data that the on path never touched.
proposed_resolution: (1) Story-writer duty: split the change so the irreversible part (an additive, backward-compatible schema or format change) ships unflagged first and the flag guards only reversible behaviour; where that is impossible, the story names each irreversible effect in a new optional key, irreversible. (2) Add to the flag-off item of F-ITEMS: nothing behind the flag has an effect that turning it off cannot undo, or the story names it. (3) For such a story, the Rollback section and the release packet say that turning the flag off does not restore the earlier state, and say what does. They never print the blanket sentence. (4) Test-writer duty: for a story that changes stored data, write a test that turns the flag on, writes, turns it off and reads.

outcome.what_was_done: The story-writer keeps behind a flag nothing that turning it off cannot undo: that part is planned as an earlier story with no flag, in a form the old code accepts, or the story names what remains in the new key flag_irreversible. The item flag-off asks that nothing behind the flag has such an effect unless the key names it. For such a story the Rollback section and the release packet print the line and not the blanket sentence. Where the on path writes stored data, the test-writer writes an off test that turns the flag on, writes, turns it off and reads.

problem: The design treats every read alike and never asks where a flag is evaluated. In a browser or mobile client, the code behind the flag ships to every user and can be read. A value evaluated on the client can be changed by whoever runs the client. The server endpoints the new feature calls can be reached whatever the flag says. So clause 2b ('can merge without being exposed') does not hold for client-evaluated flags, and the flag-off item of F-ITEMS ('no new behaviour is reachable with the flag off') would be marked checked on a client-side if. OpenFeature itself separates the two cases: its glossary ties the static-context paradigm to client-side SDKs (mobile phones, single-page web apps) and the dynamic-context paradigm to server-side SDKs. Separately, flags.key_env treats every key as a secret. Some services issue a client-side identifier that is public by design and that a client build must contain (LaunchDarkly's documentation: 'The client-side ID does not need to be kept a secret'). If such an identifier is listed in key_env, F-KEY strips it from the build and refuses any diff that contains it.
proposed_resolution: Add a decision-record heading 'Where flags are evaluated' (server, client or both, per component) and a record field evaluated (server or client). For a story behind a flag that is read on a client, the flag-off item adds three points: with the flag off, the server refuses every new endpoint and sends no new data; a client-side check is never the only guard; and the story states that the shipped client code is visible. The security-reviewer's flag-system item checks that a client-side override cannot turn on what the server does not allow. State in config/flags.md that key_env names secret keys only, so a public client identifier is configured elsewhere and a client build may carry it.

outcome.what_was_done: The decision record has the heading 'Where flags are evaluated' (server, or code that runs on a user's device, per component, and how the server enforces a flag evaluated on a device). The item flag-off asks, where the flag is read in code that runs on a user's device, that the server refuses the new behaviour too and that a check on the device is never the only guard. The item flag-system asks that a client cannot turn on what the server does not allow. flags.key_env names secret keys only, never a public identifier a client build must carry. A record field 'evaluated' was not added: where a read runs is visible in the diff the reviewer has, and a field would be a second copy an agent must keep right.

problem: Clause 6 says the factory does not create or change flags in the outside service. Two things enforce it: F-KEY removes the key variables from the commands the gates run, and F-ITEMS has the diff reviewed. An agent's own shell is covered by neither. If the person's session environment holds the service key (common when they run the product locally), every Bash command an agent runs inherits it. The secrets rule blocks printing secret-shaped variables, and it checks the web addresses and upload flags of curl, wget and http commands. It does not check request headers. It does not stop a DELETE request, which needs no upload flag. It does not cover a script in the product's language, a vendor command-line tool or a connected tool server. So 'never holds or reads its key' (sections 'Keys and secrets' and 'What the factory writes for an outside service') is a promise, not a check.
proposed_resolution: Have the hook rule secrets treat the names in flags.key_env as secret variables. It blocks a Bash segment that references one ($NAME, ${NAME}). The session briefing and vsdd doctor warn, or refuse to start a run, while one of them is set in the session environment. Where the platform allows it, drop those names from the environment of agent steps. Then rewrite the two sections to say what is enforced and what is not measured (for example, a connected tool for the service), instead of 'never'.

outcome.what_was_done: The hook rule secrets treats the names in flags.key_env as secret variables and blocks an agent's shell segment that names one; the gates remove them from what they run; vsdd status and the briefing warn while one is set in the session's environment. The sentences that said 'never' are replaced by what is enforced, and F-KEY's unmeasured cell states what is not: a program an agent runs that reads a key variable by itself, and a tool connected to the session. Refusing to start a run while a key is set was not taken: a person who runs the product locally keeps the key in their shell, and the block and the warning bound the risk without a stop. Dropping the variables from agent environments is not claimed, because the design has no verified platform fact that allows it.

problem: F-KEY's diff check searches the diff for a key's value only 'when the variable is set where the gate runs', yet the design says the factory never holds or reads the key. In the design's normal state, then, the check measures nothing. Its row does not say 'the gate reports', so it passes silently, which breaks the table's own rules: 'cannot measure' is a failure, and a limit that depends on the run is printed under metrics.flags.unmeasured. The fallback named in unmeasured, the configured scanner, runs only in the release baseline. A committed key therefore stays on the integration branch, and on any remote it was pushed to, for the rest of the cycle. Reading the variable's value also contradicts 'never ... reads its key' in topics/feature-flags.md.
proposed_resolution: Add a key flags.key_patterns: regular expressions for the shape of the flag source's secret keys. The architect chooses them and the decision record states them, so the tool names no vendor. At green, F-KEY searches added lines for these patterns and runs the configured secret scanner on the story's diff when there is one. When no key variable is set, no key pattern is configured and no scanner is configured, the gate reports 'key check not measured' under metrics.flags.unmeasured, and the release packet lists it. Reword 'never reads its key' to say what is actually true.

outcome.what_was_done: F-KEY no longer reads the value of a key variable. The new key flags.key_patterns holds the shape of the flag source's secret keys, chosen by the architect, and the green gate refuses an added line one matches. Where key_env names a variable and no pattern is configured the gate reports 'key shape not measured', which reaches the release packet. Running the general secret scanner at every green gate was not taken: that would change the green gate for every kind of secret, which D31 does not decide; the scanner stays in the release baseline.

problem: A removal is built before anyone asks the one question that decides it. The sweep turns a met removal condition into a cleanup story, which is written, tested, implemented and reviewed through the story workflow. Only after that does the merge decision ask whether the flag is on for everyone. If the answer is no, reject descopes the story, and 'the sweep proposes the removal again in the next run in which the condition still holds'. Both forms of condition hold for ever once they are met. The usual form makes this the normal case: after:<story or epic> is met when the work is done and its cycle has closed, which is when the flag ships off, not when it is on for everyone. So every maintain run rebuilds the same cleanup stories, spends maintain.fixes_per_run on them, and opens a merge decision the person rejects. That is the kind of false alarm that gets a check switched off. A separate gap: an after: condition that names a story which is later dropped is never met, so that temporary flag is never proposed for removal. F-RECORD checks only that the id exists.
proposed_resolution: Ask first. The sweep's finding puts the question to the person before any story is built: either a merge-shaped approval on the record, or the cleanup story is written but not admitted until approved. A reject must carry a new remove_when date, which the checkpoint writes into the record, so the same removal is not proposed again before that date. Describe after: as 'the work is complete', not 'safe to remove'. Where the decision record says the repository's definitions are applied, propose a removal only after a delivered flag_change: enable story. Have F-RECORD and the sweep report as a fixable traceability finding an after: condition whose story is dropped, or all of whose epic's stories are dropped.

outcome.what_was_done: Nothing is built before the question is answered: see D31R-F-4. A flag is due only when it is on, so an after: condition met while the flag ships off proposes nothing; the sweep reports such a flag as a finding that is not fixable. A reject carries until=<date> and the flag is not due again before it. artifacts/flag.md says after: states when the work is complete, not that the flag is on. F-RECORD refuses an after: that names a dropped story or an epic all of whose stories are dropped.

problem: A removal leaves dead code and fails its own gate. F-DEFINITION's removal check looks for reads only in files of class source, and for the key only in definitions files. It never looks at tests. It also cannot see the off path's old code once the read is gone, such as an unreachable else branch or an old function nobody calls. The flag's flag_off and flag_default tests from earlier stories sit in the tests class and assert the old behaviour with the flag off. Once the read is removed they fail, so the removal story's green gate fails unless someone deletes them, and the implementer may not edit tests (rules tests-first and write-scopes). No duty says to delete them. The test-writer's duty says the opposite: 'For a story that names a flag, write tests in three states'. That includes a removal story, which names the flag with flag_change: remove, while F-STATES applies only to a story with no flag_change. No review item covers a removal story.
proposed_resolution: Give the test-writer a duty for a flag_change: remove story: delete the flag's off and default tests, keep its on tests with the flag setting taken out, and write the regression test. Limit the three-state duty to a story with flag and no flag_change. Extend F-DEFINITION's removal check to the tests class: no test may still set the key (this needs the test-double pattern of D31R-D-17). Add an F-ITEMS item, flag-removed:<key>, for the adversary: the off path's code is deleted, not only the read. Cover both in F4's harness scenario 'a removal that waits for a person'.

outcome.what_was_done: The test-writer has a duty for a removal story: delete the flag's off and default tests and the test of its definition, take the flag setting out of its on tests, write the regression test. The three-state duty and F-STATES apply only to a story behind a flag (flag with no flag_change). F-DEFINITION's removal check also refuses a test that still sets the key, through the new key flags.test_patterns. The new item flag-removed:<key> has the adversary check that the code only the off state reached is deleted. F4's scenarios cover both.

problem: Lifetime is a free choice with no check and no named reviewer. A flag that guards a release can be recorded as permanent. A permanent flag needs no remove_when, creates no deferred item and is never proposed for removal: this is the classic flag that lives for ever, and the design leaves the way open. The adversary in review-stories is named to check 'each exemption, each removal condition and each default', not lifetime. The reverse mistake also does harm. A kill switch recorded as temporary is proposed for removal, and the merge packet asks whether the flag is 'on for everyone'. A kill switch usually is, so the person is invited to remove the product's emergency stop.
proposed_resolution: In F-RECORD: when the record's owning story ships behind the flag, the record is temporary unless it carries a one-line permanent_because. This holds always when flags.require asked for the flag. The plan gate lists permanent_because the way it lists flag_exempt, and the release packet prints it. Add lifetime to what the adversary checks in review-stories. The removal packet prints the record's lifetime, its title and why the flag exists, and asks 'is this a release flag that is now on for everyone?', so that a kill switch is recognised.

outcome.what_was_done: A new flag is temporary unless its record carries permanent_because and default_because; F-RECORD refuses a permanent flag without them. The plan gate lists every permanent flag with its reasons and the release packet prints them. The adversary checks each lifetime in review-stories. The removal decision's packet prints the flag's title, lifetime, the story that turned it on and the release that shipped it, and asks whether it is a release flag that is now on for everyone.

problem: Two gaps. (a) Nothing requires good behaviour at start-up or when the source is slow. The 'Defaults and failure' heading and the required contracts (the fallback when the source cannot be reached, and the kill switch) say what a read returns. They do not say whether the product starts at all while the source is down, or how long a read may wait. OpenFeature Requirement 1.1.2.4 says an SDK should offer a function that sets a provider and waits for it to initialise; that call blocks until the provider is ready or in error. The providers section of the specification sets no bound on initialisation. A product wired that way hangs at start-up while the source is unreachable. The flag_default tests set flags through an in-process test double, so they never exercise the real provider's start-up, timeout or failure. A kill switch that only takes effect at restart (a flag read once at start-up and kept) also passes every check. (b) The design says more than OpenFeature guarantees: 'the flag system returns it [the default] when the source fails'. OpenFeature defines a STALE provider status ('cached state is no longer valid and may not be up-to-date') and the resolution reasons STALE and CACHED. So after losing its source, a provider may keep answering from cached values instead of the default. The product-owner's contract 'every read returns its default when the flag source cannot be reached' is then false for the chosen system, or forces caching off.
proposed_resolution: Make the 'Defaults and failure' heading answer four cases: never reached since start (the product starts within a stated time and serves defaults); lost after start (it serves the last known values or the defaults, whichever the system does); slow (the bound on one read); and a restart during an outage. Add two contracts that flags.contracts must hold: the product starts and serves defaults while the source is unreachable; and a change to a flag's value takes effect, without a restart, within the time the 'Kill switch' heading states. Require one contract test that points the real provider at an unreachable local address (no live service) and asserts the start-up time and the fallbacks. Reword the OpenFeature sentence to match what the specification says.

outcome.what_was_done: 'Defaults and failure' now answers four cases: never reached since start, lost after start, slow, and a restart during an outage. flags.contracts is a table of four named contracts that F-CHOICE checks: fallback, startup (the product starts within a stated time while the source cannot be reached), kill_switch (a change takes effect within flags.kill_switch_seconds without a restart) and offline. The test-writer writes one test that runs the real source's client against a local address nothing listens on. The OpenFeature paragraph was checked against the specification and reworded: the default is required on abnormal execution; a provider may be STALE and a value may carry the reasons CACHED and STALE; the set-and-wait function returns when the provider is ready or in error, and the provider section sets no time limit on initialisation.

problem: The on state is tested only by the story's own flag_on tests. The rest of the suite always runs with no flag set, so existing behaviour is never checked with the flag on. Not at the story. Not when a story enables the flag: tests set flags through the test double, not through the definitions, so an enable story changes nothing any test sees. Not until a removal story makes the on path unconditional, and that happens after the person has confirmed that the flag is on for everyone in production. So if the on path breaks existing behaviour, production sees the regression before the factory's tests do. The wave and release scenarios, run with every live temporary flag on, catch only what a scenario happens to cover. The enable story also has no story kind. A kind with a red gate needs a failing test that a change to the definitions can make pass, and the suite cannot have one. A kind without a red gate tests nothing, and nothing validates the changed definitions file.
proposed_resolution: Under the 'Tests and local runs' heading, require the test double to read flags.override_env when the suite starts. The green gate of a story behind a flag, and of an enable story, then runs the suite a second time with that flag on, leaving out the flag's off and default tests, and compares that run with the baseline as well. Give the enable story a kind in flag-lifecycle.md, one without a red gate whose green gate runs this on-state suite and the definitions validation of D31R-D-18.

outcome.what_was_done: The new check F-ON runs the suite once more at the green gate of a story behind a flag, and of a story that turns a flag on, with the override variable giving that flag as true, and compares it with the baseline, leaving out the flag's off and default tests. The suite's setup must hand the override to the test double, and the gate reports when no default test changed its result. A story that turns a flag on is a feature story whose one new test reads the repository's definitions and fails until the entry serves the flag on, so it has a red gate; its green gate also runs F-ON and the definitions validation command. A kind without a red gate was not used: a docs, chore or harness story is built by an agent that may not write a file of class source, where definitions live, and facade is the kind for service clones.

problem: Reads the patterns cannot see go unreported, and some reads found later can never be recorded. A pattern finds a key only where the key is a literal at the read. New code is forced into that form, because F-USED fails a flag that nothing visibly reads. Existing code that reads flags through constants, enums or generated accessors is not. F-CHOICE's last refusal passes as soon as one literal read is found. F-FILL writes inherited records only for the keys it finds. The rest stay unrecorded and nothing reports how many there are: the check passes when it cannot measure, against clause 2a's 'a record of every flag'. F-FILL also writes inherited records only 'while the register is empty'. Once the first new record exists, a read already in the code but found later (after a person corrects the patterns, or when a member repository joins a hub) has no way to get a record, because the story-writer writes only origin: new records, which need an owning story. F-REGISTERED's whole-tree check in the wave, release and sweep jobs then fails, and nothing can clear it.
proposed_resolution: Add flags.call_patterns: expressions that match any evaluation call through the interface, whatever its key argument. A call that matches a call pattern but no read pattern is an unmeasured read. At green it is refused on added lines. Across the whole tree it is counted and listed (file and line) under metrics.flags.unmeasured. F-CHOICE compares these calls with the reads the analysis cites. Let F-FILL record as inherited any key it finds that has no record and first appears in the history before the opt-in commit, not only while the register is empty.

outcome.what_was_done: No new key was needed: a read pattern now matches every evaluation call and its group key is empty when the key is not a literal. Such an unkeyed read is refused on added lines and, on the whole tree, counted and listed (the first fifty places) under metrics.flags.unmeasured. F-CHOICE counts keyed reads, unkeyed reads and bypasses for the spec packet, and the adversary compares the patterns with the reads the analysis cites. F-FILL writes an inherited record for every key found on the integration head that has no record, at every survey, not only while the register is empty.

problem: The design does not handle existing code that has more than one flag mechanism. A common case is a vendor client in one place and hand-made switches elsewhere: environment variables, configuration booleans, a settings table. source = 'existing' assumes the analysis found one system. F-INTERFACE checks only added lines, and its row says bypasses already in the code are not seen. F-FILL records only the reads the read patterns match. So the second mechanism keeps working outside the interface, its flags are never recorded and nothing counts them. For existing code, 'one interface' and 'a record of every flag' (clause 2a) are not delivered, and nothing says so. OpenFeature offers a route the design does not use: its homepage lists 'Combine multiple solutions behind a single interface'.
proposed_resolution: Have the codebase-analyzer list every distinct flag mechanism it finds. F-CHOICE requires the decision record to name each one and say what becomes of it: adopted as the system, put behind the interface as a second provider, or migrated by named stories. Run bypass_patterns over the whole tree in the flags check of the wave, release and sweep jobs, and report the number of bypasses already in the code in metrics.flags, vsdd report debt and the release packet, so that this debt is visible and can be seen shrinking.

outcome.what_was_done: The codebase-analyzer lists every flag mechanism in a module, hand-made switches included. The decision record's 'Existing flag reads' heading must give the fate of each: kept as the system, put behind the interface as a further source, or moved by stories. A bypass pattern may capture a key, and F-FILL then records that flag as inherited. The bypass count on the whole tree is in metrics.flags.bypasses, the release packet and vsdd report debt. The OpenFeature provider that wraps several providers behind one client is named as the way a second source is put behind the interface.

problem: F-DEFINITION decides which flag a definitions change touches by finding the key's text on a changed line. In a nested format, a flag's value sits on a different line from its key. The flagd definitions format (flagd.dev) shows this: the key "new-welcome-banner" is on one line and "defaultVariant": "false" is several lines below. Two failures follow. A story that turns another flag on by changing its value line is not seen. And in JSON, adding an entry after the last one changes the previous entry's line (it gains a trailing comma), so the new flag's owning story is refused for touching a key it does not own. Both F-DEFINITION and F-USED match keys as substrings, so the key checkout is found inside checkout-v2. A key in a definitions file that has no record (a typo or an orphan) is never reported.
proposed_resolution: Attribute changes to flags by entry, not by line. Either keep one definitions file per flag where the system accepts it (the file stem is the key, so a changed file means a changed flag), or add flags.definition_patterns, an expression whose match spans one flag's whole entry and captures key. Match keys on token boundaries. In the flags check of the wave, release and sweep jobs, refuse a key in a definitions file that has no record. Where the format is multi-line and neither option is configured, report 'definitions not attributed' instead of passing.

outcome.what_was_done: F-DEFINITION attributes a change by entry: a match of flags.definition_patterns, whose group key is the flag, or with an empty list the whole of a definitions file whose stem is the key. It compares the entries at the base and at the head, so a value changed lines away from its key is seen and a neighbouring comma is not an entry. Keys are compared as captured, never as substrings. A change outside every entry is refused in a story that names no flag. In the wave, release and sweep jobs an entry whose key has no record is refused.

problem: F-INTERFACE will raise false alarms that cannot be cleared. The meaning of flags.bypass_patterns gives 'a raw read of an environment variable' as an example of a bypass. Such a pattern matches every configuration read in the product (a database address, a port), so any story that adds one fails its green gate. There is no way to mark a match as not a flag read. The implementer can only move the read into an interface file, which distorts the product, or stop, and the only real fix is a person editing approved configuration. Faced with that, people empty bypass_patterns. F-CHOICE refuses an empty list, so the remaining way out is flags.enabled = false.
proposed_resolution: Change the example to a read that the project's flag convention identifies: an environment variable with the project's flag prefix, or a call to the flag source's own client library. Give F-INTERFACE an exemption that can be reviewed: an added line that carries a fixed marker comment with a reason. The gate lists such lines under metrics.flags and the adversary checks them in review-story-diff, so a false match costs a reason and a review instead of a stop.

outcome.what_was_done: The meaning of flags.bypass_patterns now says a read that the project's flag convention names, never configuration reads in general, and the adversary checks that in review-specs. F-INTERFACE exempts an added line that carries the marker VSDD-NOT-A-FLAG: with a reason; the gate lists every marked line, and the new item not-a-flag has the adversary check each one.

problem: F-DEFAULT compares a captured fallback with the record's default only on the lines a story adds. Two existing reads with different fallbacks are never compared. Nor is a new read of an inherited flag: F-FILL writes no default, F-RECORD requires one only for origin: new, and the row does not say what happens when the record has no default. The flags check of the wave, release and sweep jobs does not run F-DEFAULT at all.
proposed_resolution: Run F-DEFAULT over the whole tree in the flags check, and report every key whose captured fallbacks disagree with each other or with the record. For an inherited record, F-FILL writes the default when all captured fallbacks agree, and reports the key when they do not. Under the 'Interface' heading, recommend one typed accessor per flag that holds its default, so each default lives in one place.

outcome.what_was_done: F-DEFAULT also runs on the whole tree in the wave, release and sweep jobs: a key whose fallbacks differ from one another or from its record is counted, and in the sweep is a fixable finding. At green a read of a flag whose record has no default is refused. F-FILL writes an inherited record's default when every captured fallback agrees and reports the keys where they do not. The recommendation of one typed accessor per flag was not taken: it is advice that no check or reviewer would hold.

problem: Flags that interact are never tested together, and the configuration a release actually ships is never evaluated end to end. Unit tests turn one flag on and leave the others at their defaults. The wave and release scenarios run with every live temporary flag on. Partial rollouts (flag A on, flag B off) are never tested. The hidden scenarios never run in the shipped configuration either, with the release's new flags off.
proposed_resolution: When the diff of a story behind a flag adds a read of another live flag, or adds a read inside a function that already reads one, require a test that names both flags' states, and add a line about the interaction to the flag-off item. At release, run the scenarios that describe existing behaviour twice: once with the shipped defaults and once with every live temporary flag on.

outcome.what_was_done: Two flags together: the item flag-off now asks, where the diff reads another flag, for a test that holds the new behaviour with that flag on and with it off; a missing one is a finding of category test. It is held by the reviewer and not by a gate, because the tests are frozen before the code that reads the second flag exists. F-ON runs the suite with the story's flag on, and vsdd env start runs wave and release with every live temporary flag on. Not taken: running the scenarios of existing behaviour a second time with the shipped defaults. The shipped state with the new flags off is the behaviour the baseline has, and the suite is compared against the baseline with no flag set at every green gate, every wave gate and the release baseline check; a second scenario evaluation would double the costliest check to measure the same thing. flag-lifecycle.md says so.

problem: Only temporary boolean flags have a checked safe default (false). For a permanent flag, or a flag that is not boolean, nothing states which way it should fail or why, and the adversary 'checks each default' with no criterion. Example: a permanent flag payments-enabled whose default is true. During an incident an operator turns it off in the service. An instance that restarts while the source is unreachable comes up with the code default, true, and payments are back on. The kill switch is undone exactly when the source is down.
proposed_resolution: Add a record field fails (open or closed) with a one-line reason, required on every permanent or non-boolean record, which the adversary checks in review-stories. Have the 'Kill switch' heading of the decision record say what a restart during an outage does to a flag that was turned off.

outcome.what_was_done: A temporary flag is boolean with the default false, so its safe value is checked by the plan gate. A permanent flag, which is the only kind that may have another type or default, must carry default_because: why its default is the value the product should run with when the source cannot be reached, a restart during an outage included. The adversary checks it in review-stories. 'Defaults and failure' in the decision record and the runbook both say what a restart during an outage does to a flag that was turned off. One line of reason was used instead of a field fails = open or closed, which would restate the default.

problem: F-STATES finds a test's state by substring: flag_on is inside flag_one, flag_off inside flag_offset and flag_default inside flag_defaults. A command-line tool's own tests about its command-line flags (for example test_flag_default_is_verbose) are counted as states, and a new one of them that is red at red fails the gate. The markers carry no key, so for a story behind two flags, or a removal story deleting one flag's tests, there is no way to tell which tests belong to which flag. A mistyped key where a test sets a flag makes an off test pass while testing nothing, and since reads are matched only in source files, nothing sees it.
proposed_resolution: Match the markers as whole tokens that include the flag key in a fixed encoded form, so a test name ties a state to a key. Add flags.test_patterns, which match a test setting a flag through the test double. Refuse a test that sets a key with no record.

outcome.what_was_done: A test's state is now the token flag_on_<k>, flag_off_<k> or flag_default_<k>, where <k> is the story's flag key encoded, with no letter or digit directly before or after it, so flag_one, flag_offset and a tool's own flag tests do not count and a test name ties a state to a key. F-RECORD refuses a new key whose encoded form equals another record's. The new key flags.test_patterns matches a test setting a flag through the test double, and F-STATES refuses an added line in which a test sets a key that has no record.

problem: The definitions in the repository can drift from the service, and nothing reports it. The service can hold flags or values the repository does not have, and repository definitions can change without ever being applied. The factory can see neither, yet the release packet still lists the 'flags this release turns on in the repository's definitions'. No command validates a changed definitions file against the flag system's format.
proposed_resolution: Under the 'Definitions and keys' heading, have the decision record state which side is authoritative and how drift is found. Where the pipeline applies definitions, the devops job includes a drift check (a dry run that fails on any difference). Where a person applies them, the release packet lists the definitions changes still to apply. Add an optional configured command that validates definitions, and run it at green whenever a definitions file changes.

outcome.what_was_done: 'Definitions and keys' in the decision record must say which is authoritative, the repository or the service, and how a difference is found. Where the pipeline applies definitions, the devops job fails on a dry run that shows a difference; the release packet lists the definition changes a person or the pipeline has still to apply. The new optional key flags.definitions_check is a command the green gate runs when a diff changes a definitions file; where it is empty the gate reports 'definitions not validated'.

problem: Tests can still reach the live service in two ways. One is a flag source that needs no key, which the row states. The other the row does not state: a product or test setup that loads its keys from a file itself, for example a .env file read at start-up, which removing variables from the environment does not affect. Neither is reported per run.
proposed_resolution: Under the 'Tests and local runs' heading, require an offline switch: a variable the gates set for every test command, which makes the wiring use the in-memory provider and open no connection to the source. A contract test of the flag system asserts it. When the switch is not configured, the gate reports that the isolation of tests is not measured.

outcome.what_was_done: The offline switch is the override variable itself, so there is one variable and it is always configured (F-CHOICE requires override_env). Its rule is the offline contract: while the variable is set, even to {}, the wiring takes flag values from it and opens no connection to the flag source, whatever keys the product or its setup could load. The gates set it for every test command and for vsdd env start, and a contract test asserts it.

problem: A reviewer can account for the flag-off item by marking it not_checkable with a reason, which convergence accepts 'when another evidence route covers it'. No other route shows that new code is unreachable with the flag off, so the item can close without anyone looking, and the row's unmeasured value 'Nothing' overstates the check. The items also apply only in loop 1: commits added in a delivery repair are reviewed as changed files, without the item.
proposed_resolution: Refuse not_checkable for the flag-off and flag-system items. Carry the flag-off item into every later review loop of a story behind a flag.

outcome.what_was_done: The same change as D31R-F-18: only checked accounts for a flag item, and flag-off and flag-removed are added again in a later loop whose commits touch a file of class source.

problem: Making every flag-removal story wait for a person adds a fourth thing that always waits, beside the three D15 lists. D15's third item, 'anything a project configures', already gives the rule a place without adding a fourth.
proposed_resolution: Make it a [flags] setting (removal merges wait for a person; default true) that falls under D15's third item, and keep the design's reason in the setting's meaning. The designer's open question 1 already asks the user about this.

outcome.what_was_done: The wait is a project setting, flags.removal (human or auto; unset reads as human), which the proposal carries and a person approves with the specification, so it falls under D15's third item. governed-delivery.md now says a flag adds nothing to the deliveries that always wait. Where the setting is human the question is asked once per flag before the removal is built (D31R-F-4).

problem: F-CHOICE runs 'always in a project that has an ingest closure', including in every sweep's spec coherence check, and it refuses a toolchain file with no flags.detected. A project whose specification was approved before the F packages ship has a locked toolchain file without that key, so every sweep would fail spec coherence until an amendment. This matters if F1 to F4 are built after cutover (the designer's open question 2), or for a project brought in by import.
proposed_resolution: Apply the refusal only to toolchain files covered by spec decisions settled after F1 ships. For older ones, report the missing key as a finding for the next amendment to fix.

outcome.what_was_done: In the sweep's spec coherence check every refusal of F-CHOICE is an advisory finding for the next amendment, so a toolchain file locked before F1 shipped, or brought in by import, fails no sweep. In vsdd gate spec it still refuses, in a run that holds an amendment and can add the key.

problem: The old pull request template's rollback section had verification steps for after the rollback and an expected recovery time, and its checklist had 'Rollback procedure validated'. The new Rollback section has only the revert and the flag-off step, so part of that capability is not ported, although the user decided that every capability ports.
proposed_resolution: Under Rollback, print the time the kill switch takes to take effect, from the decision record's 'Kill switch' heading, and the runbook's steps for verifying a rollback. Require the runbook to carry a verification heading beside 'Kill switch', and have F-RUNBOOK check it.

outcome.what_was_done: The new key flags.kill_switch_seconds is the time the kill switch takes; the kill_switch contract's test asserts it, and the Rollback section and the release packet print it. The runbook must carry a heading containing 'Verify a rollback' beside 'Kill switch'; F-RUNBOOK checks both, and the Rollback section names both.

problem: flags.standard has one value per project, and only the presence of the heading 'Why the interface is not OpenFeature' is checked. Clause 5 applies per language: in a product with several languages, OpenFeature support can differ between them. No reviewer is named to check that a value of none is justified.
proposed_resolution: Allow standard to be set per component and per member repository, beside the five path and pattern keys. Add to the architect's checked_by that the adversary verifies a none against a cited absence of an OpenFeature SDK for that language.

outcome.what_was_done: flags.standard has three values: openfeature (every language of the product), partial and none. For partial and none the heading 'Why the interface is not OpenFeature' gives the reason for each language without it, the 'Interface' heading says for each language whether an SDK exists, and the adversary checks one against the other in review-specs. A value per component or repository was not added: no program reads it, and what clause 5 needs is the reason per language, checked by a reviewer.

problem: 'Flagged' already has a meaning in this design: stories carry flags such as security. workflows/story.md says 'the story is flagged security', and workflows/plan.md and workflows/wave.md list a story's 'flags'. D31 defines 'a flagged story' as one with a feature flag key, and a builder can confuse the two.
proposed_resolution: Use 'a story behind a flag' for D31 throughout, or rename the existing usage, and define the term once in conventions.md.

outcome.what_was_done: Closed by the same rename as D31R-F-19: the overlay is story-behind-flag. The definition of 'story behind a flag' stays in the glossary.

problem: Read patterns are 'matched against the whole text of a file, so a read may span lines', but F-REGISTERED, F-INTERFACE and F-DEFAULT run 'on added lines' without saying how a match over the whole file is tied to added lines. The regular-expression dialect is not stated, and the syntax of named groups differs between engines. A whole-file expression that backtracks heavily has no time bound.
proposed_resolution: State that a match counts when its span overlaps an added line. Name the engine (the tool's own) and its named-group syntax in the key's meaning, with an example, and compile the patterns when the configuration loads. Bound the matching time per file, and report a timeout as 'cannot measure'.

outcome.what_was_done: config/flags.md has a section 'Patterns': the syntax is Python's re module, with (?P<key>...) for a named group; where each kind of pattern is matched; a match belongs to a story's added lines when its span includes a character of an added line; the loader compiles every pattern and a failure is a configuration error naming the key; the scan of one file is stopped after five seconds and reported as 'cannot measure', which the header of flag-checks.toml makes a failure. The scanner is built once, in F1.

problem: Clause 7 asks that no code reads a flag outside the one interface, and clause 2(a) and 5 ask for one interface, which matters most for existing code. The design checks only added lines (F-INTERFACE at green). The flags check of the wave, release and sweep jobs runs F-REGISTERED and F-USED but no bypass search. So reads that existing code makes straight through a vendor SDK are never counted, reported or planned away. F-INTERFACE states this as unmeasured. After opting in, an ingested product keeps two ways of reading flags indefinitely: the old direct reads and the new interface. Nothing asks the architect, product-owner or story-writer to move them. The same gap covers the case flag-system-choice.md describes, where flags are detected and the person names another system: the record 'says how the code moves off the old one', but no heading, check or story holds that.
proposed_resolution: Add F-INTERFACE on the whole tree to the flags check of wave, release and sweep. It reports every bypass match outside flags.interface as a fixable finding (category code, owner implementer) and lists the count in the release packet and report-debt. For source = existing, and for detected = true with source = named, require a decision-record heading 'Reads outside the interface' that states the count found on the integration head and how they move behind the interface. Give the story-writer the duty to plan those moves as stories after the interface story. F-CHOICE checks that the heading exists.

outcome.what_was_done: F-INTERFACE now also runs on the whole tree in the flags check of wave, release and sweep: it records the number of unmarked bypass matches outside the interface (metrics.flags.bypasses), and in the sweep each is a fixable finding of category code, so maintain moves the reads behind the interface within maintain.fixes_per_run. The release packet and vsdd report debt print the figure. The decision record needs the heading 'Existing flag reads' whenever detected is true (source existing, or named with a system found): every mechanism found, its fate, the count F-CHOICE measured and how the reads move. F-CHOICE refuses a record without it and counts keyed reads, unkeyed reads and bypasses for the spec packet. The story-writer plans the moves that need a design; the adversary checks them in review-stories.

problem: Clause 2(b) asks for 'default off', so that half-finished work can merge without being exposed. The design holds the fallback at the read (F-RECORD, F-DEFAULT) but not the value the definition serves. F-DEFINITION states 'what a definition says' as unmeasured. flag-lifecycle.md 'Delivered off' cites F-USED, F-RECORD, F-STATES and F-ITEMS, and none of them checks the definition's value. The implementer's row in flag-duties.toml says the flag-off item holds it to 'write its definition, default off', but the flag-off item's text in F-ITEMS does not mention the definition. Where the decision record says the pipeline applies definitions, an owning story whose definition serves 'on' exposes the feature on merge, and nothing catches it.
proposed_resolution: Add to the flag-off:<key> item of F-ITEMS, and to the adversary's duty, that the definition the owning story writes serves the off value (the record's default) in every environment it defines. Optionally, let the toolchain carry a definition_off_pattern that F-DEFINITION matches on the owning story's added definition lines, failing with 'cannot measure' when it is empty.

outcome.what_was_done: The item flag-off now asks that the owning story's definition serves the default in every environment it defines, and the implementer's duty says so. Where a definition pattern captures the named group value, F-DEFINITION refuses an owning story's entry whose value differs from the record's default; where none does, the gate reports 'definition value not measured' and the item is the evidence.

problem: In a project that has not opted in, the story-writer must return blocked with kind spec_gap whenever it judges that a story cannot merge safely without a flag. That opens a spec-gap stop, which halts the whole plan workflow because its gate needs every epic done. Clause 3 says a project that has not opted in is not forced into flags, and the decision is asked once. The design does not record a not-a-gap answer, a person-written flags.enabled = false or a toolchain 'declined' as the project's standing answer. So every later story, and every later amendment in which the architect may propose flags again, can ask the same question. This conflicts with clause 3, with clause 4's 'asked once ... so that later stories do not ask again', and with the low-touch rule that a stop exists only where a person must decide.
proposed_resolution: Ask once and record the answer. The story-writer may raise the flags spec_gap only while the project has never answered: flags.enabled is unset in factory.toml, no toolchain 'declined' exists, and no earlier spec-gap on flags was settled. A not-a-gap on that gap, a declined text, or a person-set enabled = false then stands for the project. The story-writer and the architect do not raise or propose flags again until a person asks through a request or the brief. Otherwise the story goes ahead unflagged, and the plan gate result notes what the setting would have flagged.

outcome.what_was_done: No story stops for a flag any more: the spec_gap path is removed. A project is in one of three computed states (off, requested, on). While flags are not on the story-writer names no flag and stops for none, and the plan gate lists under metrics.flags.would_require the stories the setting would have asked for. The standing answer is flags.enabled having a value: written by a person, or copied by the survey from the approved proposal (true with flags=<source>, false with flags=decline or a declined text). A false stands: the architect proposes a flag system only when the code has one, a person asks (brief, request, guidance) or the state is requested, and never again after a decline until a person asks.

problem: The removal stop is a fourth always-wait that neither D15 nor D31 lists, and as designed it repeats. The cleanup story is built in full (tests, review, green gate) before the person is asked. A reject descopes it, and 'the sweep proposes the removal again in the next run in which the condition still holds'. With remove_when = date: or after:, which say nothing about whether the flag is on in production, a flag still off for users is rebuilt and re-asked in every maintain run until the person edits remove_when through the author skill. Each answer is the same, so most of these stops are not needed, and the rebuilt story each run is wasted work.
proposed_resolution: Ask once per flag, and ask before building. When the condition is met, the sweep's finding opens the question ('is <key> on for everyone?'). Only an approve writes the cleanup story, and its merge then follows delivery.merge. A reject takes a new condition (for example -- until <date>), which the record keeps, so the sweep is silent until then. Where a delivered flag_change: enable story turned the flag on in the repository's definitions and the decision record says the pipeline applies them, the factory knows the flag is on, and no person is needed. Leave the user's open question about automatic removal as it is.

outcome.what_was_done: A removal is asked once per flag and before anything is written. A flag is due only when its remove_when is met and it is on (a delivered flag_change: enable story whose cycle has closed), so a flag that ships off is never proposed. Where flags.removal is human the checkpoint opens one merge decision named for the flag (merge.flag-<stem>); approve lets the next maintain run write the cleanup story, which then merges as delivery.merge says; reject needs until=<date> (F-APPROVE) and the flag is not due again before that day. Where flags.removal is auto, which the proposal may say only where the repository's definitions are authoritative and the pipeline applies them, no person is asked. The delivery refusal and the always-wait at story deliver are gone. A person's own removal request waits for no decision.

problem: Clause 5 wants the vendor changeable later, and flag-system-choice.md says a person changes the system with a change request whose new decision record a spec decision approves. But F-FILL copies the run keys (interface, read_patterns, bypass_patterns, definitions, runbook, key_env, override_env) into factory.toml only while they are unset, and never overwrites a set key. It cannot tell a key the survey filled from one a person set. After the first approval those keys are set, so a superseding toolchain never reaches factory.toml. The gates keep checking the old system's patterns and interface while flags.decision names the new record. F-REGISTERED and F-INTERFACE then pass or fail against the wrong system.
proposed_resolution: Keep one source. Either leave the run keys out of factory.toml and have the loader read them from the latest approved toolchain file unless a person has set them in factory.toml, or have the survey record which keys it filled and refresh exactly those from each newly approved toolchain, announcing the change in the briefing. Have the spec packet show any person-set [flags] key that will override the approved proposal.

outcome.what_was_done: The approved settings have one source. factory.toml gets a table [flags.approved] that only the survey writes: a copy of the [flags] table of the toolchain file the latest approved spec decision covers, rewritten whenever the two differ and announced in the briefing with each key that changed. A check reads a key from [flags] when a person wrote it there and from [flags.approved] otherwise, so a superseding proposal reaches every gate at the next survey and no value a person set is rewritten. vsdd status, the briefing and the next spec packet list every override.

problem: 'Enabled but not configured' (a person sets flags.enabled = true in factory.toml without a chosen system) makes every flags check in every gate fail with 'cannot measure'. F-REGISTERED and F-INTERFACE run on added lines at every story's green gate, so every story in the open cycle stops, flagged or not. The remedy the file names is a change request for the flag system, run as an amendment. But feature needs a baseline (a release, an approved ingest or an import), and a non-critical request stays queued while another cycle is active. In a first cycle the remedy cannot run, and the cycle cannot finish. Missing [commands], the case this is compared to, is a precondition of the workflows that measure, not a failure inside every gate.
proposed_resolution: Treat it as missing commands is treated. Flag checks on a story that names no flag report 'flags not configured' in the gate result and the release packet instead of failing. The plan gate refuses only stories that name a flag. vsdd status and the briefing show the state. The remedy inside an open cycle is the spec-gap amend path (the plan gate or the story-writer raises a spec_gap on 'flags enabled, no system'), and outside a cycle it is the change request.

outcome.what_was_done: 'Enabled but not configured' is now the state requested: a person wrote enabled = true and no approved proposal names a system. In that state everything is as in off, so no flag check runs and no gate fails; a story that names a flag is refused at the plan gate; vsdd status, the briefing, every gate result and the release packet report it; and the architect proposes the system the next time it writes architecture. The amend path inside an open cycle was not added: nothing is blocked in that state, so the open cycle finishes and the change request for the flag system runs after it like any request. 'Cannot measure' stays a failure only while flags are on, where the cause is one key a person can correct in factory.toml.

problem: Clause 6: tests run without reaching the live service. F-KEY removes key variables only from commands a gate or vsdd env start launches. The implementer and test-writer have SHELL and run the suite in their own shells during TDD, with the session's environment. Where the product's wiring installs the real provider when a key is present, a flag_default test ('sets nothing') and the rest of the suite reach the live service. The test-writer's row in flag-duties.toml says the adversary checks this in review-story-diff, but the adversary's own row and the F-ITEMS items do not include it. flags.override_env is not removed from gate commands either, so a value left set in the shell where the gate runs can turn flags on for the whole suite.
proposed_resolution: Make the test setup carry the guarantee. The decision record's 'Tests and local runs' heading must name how the suite installs the in-memory test double for every test under the test command, so no network provider runs there whatever the environment. Add 'no test reaches the live flag service, and the suite's setup installs the test double' to the flag-system item and to the flag-off item, and to the adversary's duty. Have F-KEY also remove flags.override_env from every gate command except vsdd env start.

outcome.what_was_done: The decision record's 'Tests and local runs' heading must name the suite-wide setup that installs the test double for every test, whatever the environment holds, and gives it the values of the override variable. The new offline contract states that while the override variable is set the wiring opens no connection to the flag source. The items flag-off (no test reaches the flag service, flags set only through the test double) and flag-system (the suite's setup installs the double for every test) hold it, and the adversary's and security-reviewer's rows carry the text. F-KEY now sets the override variable itself for every command a gate runs ({} for a test command) and never passes on a value inherited from the shell.

problem: Clause 5 makes OpenFeature the interface wherever the product's language supports it. F-CHOICE only checks that, with standard = "none", the heading 'Why the interface is not OpenFeature' has text under it. The adversary's review-specs duty covers the source of the choice, a researched choice's alternatives and the read patterns, but not whether the reason for none holds. A language that has a maintained SDK can still end with standard = none.
proposed_resolution: Add to the architect row's checked_by, and to the adversary's review-specs duty: check the standard = none reason against the SDK availability and maturity the 'Interface' heading states.

outcome.what_was_done: The 'Interface' heading must say, for each language of the product, whether an OpenFeature SDK exists. The architect's checked_by now has the adversary, in review-specs, check a standard other than openfeature against that statement, language by language.

problem: Clause 7 says a flagged story's contract covers both states. The design covers both states in tests (F-STATES) but does not require the story's acceptance criteria to state them. The story-writer's duty is silent on it. So the off and default tests trace to no criterion, and the criterion-to-test map and the demo table do not show the off state.
proposed_resolution: Give the story-writer the duty to write, for a story behind a flag, a criterion for the off and default states (existing behaviour unchanged) beside the criteria for the on state. Name the tests ac<N>_flag_off and so on, and have F-REQUIRE refuse a story behind a flag with no off-state criterion.

outcome.what_was_done: The story-writer writes criteria for both states: the new behaviour with the flag on, and a criterion containing the words 'flag off' for the behaviour that stays. F-REQUIRE refuses a story behind a flag with no such criterion. F-STATES refuses an off or default test whose name names no criterion (ac<N>), so the criterion-to-test map shows the off state.

problem: Rule 1 (one fact, one place) is broken in several places. The header of flag-checks.toml says outright that a permanent limit 'is stated here and in [[topic:feature-flags]]'. feature-flags.md restates the definition of high-risk (config/flags.md), the decision record's soundness list (flag-system-choice.md), where the record and definitions live (artifacts/flag.md) and the F-KEY behaviour (also restated in config/flags.md and the flag-config-keys meaning). The restatements have already drifted: feature-flags.md says an after: condition is met when the story or epic is 'done and released', while artifacts/flag.md says 'done and the cycle that delivered it has closed'.
proposed_resolution: Keep each fact in its home and link to it: the limits in the unmeasured cells, high-risk in config/flags.md, the headings in flag-system-choice.md, the record in artifacts/flag.md, the key handling in F-KEY. Cut feature-flags.md's 'What was decided, and why' to the reasons and the links. Settle the after: wording in artifacts/flag.md only.

outcome.what_was_done: Each of the three restatements is gone, and two more of the same kind that a search found. (1) 'The tool never reads the value of a key variable' is deleted from config/flags.md 'Keys and local runs'; the fact stays in F-KEY's reads cell. (2) Which table a check reads, [flags] before [flags.approved], stays in config/flags.md 'Who writes it' and nowhere else: the header of flag-config-keys.toml now says only that override = true marks a key a person may also write, with a link to config:flags, and 'and wins' is cut from the meaning of flags.enabled. (3) The moved-test rule keeps its reason in feature-flags.md 'Why it is this way' and its rule in the test-writer's duty, F-STATES and F-ON. flag-lifecycle.md 'Delivered off' is cut to a link to the duty and F-STATES, 'Who turns a flag on' names F-ON instead of restating its refusal of a pending test, and step 6 of feature-flags.md no longer restates the move. Also: where a person overrides a member repository's flag values is now only in the row flags.repo.<name> (config/flags.md links to it), and that the spec packet lists overrides is now only in flag-system-choice.md.

problem: The section 'What ports from the old plugin' is a mapping from the old system, which rule 6 puts in rewrite/history/, not in the spec. The port itself holds. The delivery skill's 'feature flag wrapping recommended for high-risk changes' becomes flags.require = high-risk. The template's rollback instructions, its Flag/Controls/Default table and its 'Feature flag configured' checklist line become the Rollback section, the Feature flags section and F-USED.
proposed_resolution: Move the mapping to rewrite/history/ or to a ledger entry; keep only the two pull request sections in the spec.

outcome.what_was_done: The section is removed from the spec. rewrite/history/ is outside what this step may edit, so the mapping is recorded here. (1) The old delivery skill's line 'Feature flag wrapping recommended for high-risk changes' (plugins/vsdd-factory/skills/code-delivery/SKILL.md) is the setting flags.require, default high-risk, applied by F-REQUIRE. (2) The old pull request template's 'Rollback Instructions' (the revert, 'If feature-flagged' with its expected recovery time, 'Verification after rollback') is the Rollback section in every pull request body, with flags.kill_switch_seconds and the runbook heading 'Verify a rollback'. (3) Its 'Feature Flags' table (Flag, Controls, Default) is the Feature flags section. (4) Its checklist line 'Feature flag configured' is F-USED, and 'Rollback procedure validated' is the kill_switch contract's test with F-RUNBOOK.

problem: Lines 13 and 25 (the delivers of F2 and F4) are 401 and 408 characters, over the 400-character limit of rule 4. spec_lint passes because it skips registry.d/ when it checks line length.
proposed_resolution: Shorten the two delivers strings (for example, move 'One failing and one passing case per refusal' to the package Notes), and consider having spec_lint check registry.d/ lines.

outcome.what_was_done: The integrator shortened the two delivers strings. The orchestrating session also made spec_lint apply the 400-character line limit to files in registry.d/, which it used to skip.

problem: F2 is not sized for one builder. It covers 13 checks with about 40 refusal clauses, each needing a failing and a passing case. It wires them into eight commands owned by eight packages (G1, G2, G3, G5, G6a, G6b, G7, G4a), plus the verdict items and the survey and admission change of D31-8. There is also a dependency inversion. F-FILL, built by F1, writes inherited records from the read patterns, but the pattern scanner is part of the 'one module the gates call' that F2 builds after F1.
proposed_resolution: Split F2 into a planning part (F-CHOICE, F-RECORD, F-REQUIRE, F-READY in the G5 gates) and a story and job part (F-STATES to F-KEY, F-RUNBOOK, F-REMOVE, F-ITEMS). Put the read-pattern scanner (compile, match, capture key and default, class source only) in F1, so F-FILL and the F2 checks share it.

outcome.what_was_done: The checks are now three packages and three tables: F5 builds the checks of choosing and planning (F-CHOICE, F-RECORD, F-REQUIRE, F-READY; table flag-checks), F2 the checks of a story's gates and review (table flag-story-checks; it keeps ledger entry D31-8), F6 the flags check of the wave, release and sweep jobs with F-RUNBOOK and F-REMOVE (table flag-release-checks). The pattern scanner (compile, bounded match, named groups, added lines) is in F1, so F-FILL and every later check share it. The ids F5 and F6 were added rather than renumbering, because the ledger's triage names F2, F3 and F4; the build plan gives the order F1, F5, F2, F6, F3, F4.

problem: F4's scenarios run a story through story, a story refused at the plan gate, a removal that waits in maintain, and one story-tier run. Yet F4 depends on none of W2, W5 or W6, W11 or E2; it relies only on the 'workflows follow' ordering. The build plan places E1 in step 6, after the F packages, although F4 depends on E1. Only E1's first part, which the slice builds, is meant.
proposed_resolution: Add W2, W5 (or W6), W11 and E2 to F4's depends. In the build plan, say F4 needs E1's first part and E2's story tier, both built on the slice.

outcome.what_was_done: F4 now depends on W2, W5, W6, W11 and E2 as well. Its delivers text and the build plan's order of work say it needs only the first part of E1 and the story tier of E2, both of which the slice builds.

problem: The flag row introduces artifact-registry semantics that the shipped format does not have, and the ledger does not name them. A 'stem' column percent-encodes the key, so the id no longer equals the file stem, against the shipped header's rule that id equals the stem. Freezing on 'removed' is a lock condition outside the existing 'spec' and 'done'. The deferred item 'deferred/flag-<key>.md' is built from the raw key, which for an inherited key may hold '/', capitals or spaces. state-layout.md writes the path as stories/flags/<key>.md. The [toolchain] row caps the file at 4,000 bytes, which a [flags] table of pattern and glob lists, unioned across components, can exceed.
proposed_resolution: Widen D31-1 (and its by-package entry for F1, which depends on H4) to name the artifact-rule changes: the stem column and its check, a 'removed' lock, deferred items named from the stem, state-layout written with <stem>, and a raised [toolchain] max_bytes.

outcome.what_was_done: Recorded again with its outcome unchanged, because the correction of d31-fix-2-C1-1 added a second way to remove a flag and the earlier text named one. The design is settled in the spec; the shipped artifact registry (next/plugins/vsdd-factory/py/vsdd/policy/artifacts.toml) and the artifact rule must follow it when package F1 is built, in the same change as D31-1. F1 adds: the stem cell of the [flag] row and the check that a record's path is its key percent-encoded (the id no longer equals the stem); the lock value removed (frozen once a delivered story removes the flag, with flag_change: remove or withdraw); the fourth story key flag_irreversible and the record keys permanent_because and default_because, as artifacts/flag.md gives them; the [deferred-item] writer vsdd checkpoint, with the item named deferred/flag-<stem>.md; and a [toolchain] cap of 12,000 bytes. The spec side is done: artifacts/flag.md states the two format additions, flag-lifecycle.md and state-layout.md use <stem>, and artifacts/toolchain.md states the cap.

problem: 'Keys and secrets' relies on the secrets hook rule to keep agents from printing key variables. That rule blocks echo or printf of a 'secret-shaped' variable and web calls carrying such values. A variable named in flags.key_env need not be secret-shaped, so the claim may not hold. No ledger entry asks the secrets rule (package H2) to treat the key_env names as secret.
proposed_resolution: Add a ledger entry for H2, taken by F2: the secrets rule treats every name in flags.key_env as secret-shaped (for printing, and for the web-call and upload value checks), with one case each.

outcome.what_was_done: rules/secrets.md has a section for decision D31: in a project that uses flags the variables flags.key_env names are secret variables whatever their names look like, and the rule blocks a shell segment that names one. The rule is not built yet, so the spec file is where its builder reads this; the section says it is built with package F2, whose delivers text and dependency on H2 carry it. No ledger entry is needed, because no shipped file has to change.

problem: Ledger entry D31-7 (the registry summary of decisions.md) is triaged to package F1 with the outcome left-for-builder. Its own text says it is not a builder's edit, and only the orchestrating session may change registry.toml. So F1's by-package list holds a task its builder is not allowed to do.
proposed_resolution: Triage D31-7 to no package, as an orchestrator item, and leave its outcome open until the orchestrating session changes the summary.

outcome.what_was_done: D31-7 is triaged to no package (triage/d31.json), its left-for-builder outcome is removed from outcomes/d31.json, and the registry summary it asked for is changed, so no builder's list carries it.

problem: F-ITEMS accepts an item marked not_checkable with a reason, so a reviewer can close flag-off:<key> or flag-system without looking, although the diff is always there to check. Items count only in loop 1. A later loop after a delivery repair checks only the changed files, so new commits that make code reachable with the flag off are not re-checked against the item.
proposed_resolution: For flag-off and flag-system require the state checked; not_checkable counts as uncovered and goes to a finding decision at the cap. In a later loop, carry flag-off:<key> again when the new commits touch files of class source.

outcome.what_was_done: F-ITEMS accepts only checked for its items; not_checkable does not account for one and the item then counts as uncovered. In a later review loop the items flag-off and flag-removed are added again when the commits that loop reviews touch a file of class source.

problem: The term 'flagged' collides with the existing design. artifacts/flag.md defines 'a flagged story' as one with flag and no flag_change. But workflows/story.md already says 'the story is flagged security' (security: true), and plan.md and wave.md use 'flags' for the story's boolean keys. A builder reading the story script can confuse the two.
proposed_resolution: Name D31's term 'a story behind a flag' throughout the flag files, or rename the existing uses to 'marked security' and 'story keys'.

outcome.what_was_done: The fixture overlay in F4's delivers text is renamed story-behind-flag and the briefs are regenerated. No file under rewrite/spec/ or next/ names story-flagged any more.

problem: Opting in (clause 3) and confirming the system (clause 4) both ride on a plain approve of the whole specification set. The packet prints the flag lines, but a person who approves a large set confirms the flag system without ever naming it. Declining a system that ingest found costs a full revise round and a second spec stop, because only the architect can write declined.
proposed_resolution: When an approval would turn flags.enabled from false to true, have F-APPROVE require a named value on approve (for example flags=existing, flags=named or flags=researched, matching source), as it already does for home-built. That keeps the confirmation explicit with no new stop. Consider flags=decline -- <words> as a way to decline a found system at the same stop.

outcome.what_was_done: F-APPROVE refuses a plain approve of a specification that would accept the flag decision record: the person types approve flags=<source>, where the value is the proposal's source (existing, named, researched, home-built). For a system found in existing code, approve flags=decline -- <words> approves the specification and leaves flags off without a revise round. Declining a new system is still revise, because its contracts, decision record and dependency are in the set and approval changes no file.

problem: F-CHOICE's last refusal (with source = existing, read patterns that find no read on the integration head) also runs inside the sweep's spec coherence check, in every project with an ingest closure. Once the last flag has been removed, or the code moved to new reads with other patterns, every sweep fails spec coherence against an approved, locked toolchain file that no maintenance fix can change.
proposed_resolution: Apply the 'patterns find reads' refusal only when gate spec checks a proposal that is not yet approved (the run that proposes it). In the sweep, report it as an advisory.

outcome.what_was_done: Inside the sweep's spec coherence check every refusal of F-CHOICE is an advisory finding for the next amendment: the set is locked there and no maintenance fix can change it. The 'patterns find reads' refusal is now 'with detected true, read and bypass patterns that between them match nothing', and it refuses only in vsdd gate spec, in a run that can change the proposal.

problem: F-RUNBOOK fails the release baseline check when the runbook is missing, and the finding becomes a docs fix story. No duty plans the runbook when the flag system is built. The story-writer's row covers the interface and the owning stories only. So the first verify after opting in always fails on it and needs a fix round.
proposed_resolution: Give the story-writer the duty to plan a docs story for flags.runbook alongside the stories that cite flag-system contracts, and order a story behind a flag after it, or after the kill-switch story.

outcome.what_was_done: The story-writer plans a docs story for the runbook with the stories that build the flag system, and orders a story behind a flag after it. F-READY refuses a story behind a flag while the runbook is not on the integration head unless its depends_on chain reaches a docs story that cites the kill_switch contract.

problem: The architect's duty includes 'state in conventions.md that a flag is read only through the interface with its key as a literal', but lists only the method architecture. conventions.md belongs to the method conventions (guidance class, with its own lock, outside the spec decision's digest). So L-FLAG would place the section in the wrong method, and the rule would not be part of what the spec approval confirms.
proposed_resolution: Either add conventions to the architect's methods for this duty, or put the rule under the decision record's 'Interface' heading, which the spec decision approves, and have the conventions method link to it.

outcome.what_was_done: The architect's duty no longer writes conventions.md. The rule that a flag is read only through the interface with its key as a literal is under the decision record's 'Interface' heading, which the spec decision approves, and in the implementer's own duty.

problem: flag-lifecycle.md puts the Rollback section 'in every pull request', including projects that never opted in, but story-deliver.md and F3's delivers call it one of 'the two flag sections' without saying that. It is the port of the old template's rollback, which was not about flags. A builder of F3 or G4a cannot tell whether a project that has not opted in gets it.
proposed_resolution: Say in story-deliver.md that Rollback is in every pull request body and that the flag step is added only for a story behind a flag. Or assign the plain Rollback section to G4a's body renderer and keep only its flag line in F3.

outcome.what_was_done: flag-lifecycle.md and story-deliver.md now say the same: Rollback is in every pull request of every project, whatever its flag state, with a flag step only for a story that names a flag; Feature flags is for a story that names a flag. Package F3 adds both, because the body renderer of G4a is on the slice path and may not change before the build widens.

problem: Decision D31 adds one artifact kind and four story keys that the shipped registry does not hold. Until it does, a flag record under .factory/stories/flags/ matches no kind and is blocked by [_unknown]; a story that carries flag, flag_change, flag_exempt or flag_irreversible fails its frontmatter check; a toolchain file with a [flags] table is outside the [toolchain] row's description and over its cap; and the [deferred-item] row names the defer skill as the only writer, although the checkpoint must write one item, deferred/flag-<stem>.md, for each live temporary flag. The [flag] row also needs two things the registry's format lacks: a stem cell, because a record's path is its key percent-encoded and so the id no longer equals the file stem; and the lock value removed.
proposed_resolution: Add the [flag] row and [flag.frontmatter] exactly as rewrite/spec/artifacts/flag.md gives them, with the stem cell and its check, the lock value removed and the keys permanent_because, default_because and repo, and with the skeleton templates/flag.md. Add four optional keys to [story.frontmatter]: flag = "str?", flag_change (enable, remove or withdraw), flag_exempt = "str?" and flag_irreversible = "str?". Name the [flags] table in the [toolchain] row and raise that row's cap to 12,000 bytes. Add vsdd checkpoint to the [deferred-item] writer. Extend the pins in tests/unit/test_policy.py. Then shrink rewrite/spec/artifacts/flag.md to a pointer at the shipped row. D31R-F-15 names the same format additions; one change closes both.

outcome.what_was_done: The design is settled in rewrite/spec/artifacts/flag.md, which carries the row to add, the stem cell, the lock value removed and the four story keys. Package F1 adds the row, the story keys and the two widened rows ([toolchain], [deferred-item]) to the shipped registry as its first task, when the build widens past the thin slice.
